cues.text: Welcome to Organic Halogens.
This recorded Chemistry class uses an AI generated Marin voice.
Classify the carbon bearing halogen before comparing reactions.
In a haloalkane, halogen is bonded to a saturated carbon.
In chlorobenzene, chlorine is directly attached to an aromatic ring carbon.
In benzyl chloride, chlorine is attached to a carbon outside the ring, so the
reacting environment is different.
Primary, secondary and tertiary alkyl halides are classified by how many
carbons are attached to the carbon carrying halogen.
A carbon halogen bond is generally polarized toward halogen, leaving the
carbon
susceptible to suitable nucleophiles.
Bond strength, leaving group stability, steric access and solvent all affect
reactivity.
For comparable simple substrates in many substitution settings, iodide is a
better leaving group than bromide, which is better than chloride; fluoride is
generally poor.
This ranking cannot replace a stated mechanism or conditions.
Also distinguish allylic and benzylic centres from vinylic and aryl centres.
A nearby pi system can stabilize an intermediate, but direct attachment to an
unsaturated carbon creates a different substitution problem.
Several routes produce organic halides, and they do not all use the same
mechanism.
Suitable hydrogen halides or reagents such as thionyl chloride can replace an
alcohol's hydroxyl group under appropriate conditions.
Adding hydrogen halide to an alkene instead consumes a pi bond and adds
hydrogen and halogen.
Radical halogenation of an alkane uses initiating conditions and can give
mixtures.
Aromatic ring halogenation commonly uses an electrophilic pathway with a
suitable Lewis acid.
In toluene, chlorine with iron three chloride under ring substitution
conditions can introduce chlorine on the ring, with ortho and para
preferences.
Under radical conditions such as light, substitution can instead occur at the
side chain.
Do not infer the reaction site from the molecular formula of the reagent
alone.
Preparation may also cause elimination, rearrangement or further substitution
depending on substrate and conditions.
Before writing an arrow, circle the carbon being changed and identify whether
the intended process replaces a group, adds across a multiple bond or changes
a
side chain.
Then verify the product's carbon skeleton.
In the S N two mechanism, a nucleophile approaches carbon from the side
opposite the leaving group.
Bond formation and departure occur in one concerted step.
A free carbocation is not an intermediate.
In the simple rate law, rate equals the rate constant times substrate
concentration times nucleophile concentration.
Doubling either concentration doubles the rate, and doubling both multiplies
it
by four, with temperature and other conditions unchanged.
Backside access becomes harder as the reaction centre is crowded.
Comparable methyl and primary alkyl substrates are therefore more accessible
than tertiary substrates for this pathway.
Polar aprotic solvents often support reactive anionic nucleophiles, although
the complete substrate and reagent combination must still be considered.
At a reacting stereogenic carbon, backside attack inverts the local geometry.
This does not automatically turn every R label into S, because priority
rankings may change in the product.
Reassign the configuration rather than treating a label as a physical
mechanism.
A stronger nucleophile cannot simply force an ordinary tertiary centre to
follow a favourable backside substitution path.
In a simple S N one mechanism, slow ionization first forms a carbocation
and leaving group.
Nucleophile capture occurs afterward.
The ideal rate law depends on substrate concentration alone, because
nucleophile participation is not part of the slow ionization step.
Doubling only nucleophile concentration therefore produces no direct rate
change in this ideal model.
A tertiary substrate can favour ionization under suitable conditions because
its carbocation is more stable than a simple primary one.
Benzylic and allylic intermediates may gain resonance stabilization.
Strongly ionizing media can assist separation of charged species.
A carbocation can rearrange when a more favourable structure is accessible, so
compare skeletons before declaring the final substitution product.
A planar carbocation permits attack from either face, allowing a stereogenic
substrate to lose optical purity.
Exact equal racemization is not guaranteed because ion pairing and nearby
groups can make the faces unequally accessible.
These are mechanistic tendencies, not a rule that every tertiary halide always
gives substitution: elimination can compete.
State the solvent, nucleophile and temperature before choosing a dominant
pathway.
In beta elimination, hydrogen is removed from a carbon adjacent to the carbon
carrying the leaving group.
A double bond forms between these alpha and beta carbons.
In the E two mechanism, base removes hydrogen as the leaving group departs in
the same step.
The simple rate depends on both substrate and base concentrations.
An appropriate anti periplanar arrangement helps the required orbital overlap;
ring conformations can therefore restrict which product forms.
Heating a suitable haloalkane with alcoholic potassium hydroxide commonly
favours elimination in elementary questions, while aqueous hydroxide often
favours substitution for suitable substrates.
These are contextual comparisons, not absolute switches.
Bromoethane with aqueous hydroxide can give ethanol; with hot alcoholic base
it
can give ethene.
A secondary butyl halide with a small base often gives but two ene as the
major
alkene, while bulky bases or geometric restrictions can change preferences.
First check that a beta hydrogen exists, then identify all possible adjacent
double bonds.
Distinguish the major product from the only possible product.
Ordinary chlorobenzene resists the usual alkyl substitution pathways.
The chlorine bearing carbon is sp two hybridized, and conjugation gives the
carbon chlorine bond partial double bond character.
Ordinary backside S N two displacement at that aromatic carbon is difficult.
A simple S N one route would require an unfavourable phenyl cation, so it is
not the usual alternative.
Benzyl chloride has its leaving group on a saturated carbon outside the ring
and must be considered separately.
Resistance does not mean all haloarenes are chemically inert.
Strong electron withdrawing groups, such as nitro groups in suitable ortho or
para positions relative to halogen, can activate a ring toward nucleophilic
aromatic substitution.
The intermediate and reaction pathway differ from ordinary alkyl substitution.
A meta nitro group does not provide the same direct resonance stabilization in
the usual addition elimination mechanism.
Harsh conditions can also allow other aromatic substitution pathways.
For an exam comparison, mark the exact attachment point, locate activating
substituents and read the conditions before ranking reactivity from a
memorized
halide list.
An appropriate organic halide can react with magnesium in dry ether to form a
Grignard reagent.
Its carbon has strongly basic and nucleophilic character.
Water or another sufficiently acidic proton can quench the reagent before a
planned carbon carbon bond forming reaction.
Ethylmagnesium bromide meeting water gives ethane as its organic product: the
ethyl carbon accepts a proton instead of adding to a later carbonyl reagent.
This is why dry conditions are chemically necessary.
When no acidic interference is present, reaction with an appropriate carbonyl
compound followed by work up can form a new carbon carbon bond, but the
precise
product depends on the carbonyl partner.
Wurtz coupling instead uses sodium with suitable alkyl halides in dry ether.
Two methyl halide units can couple to ethane.
Using different alkyl halides can give several homo and cross coupling
products, making the method poorly selective for one unsymmetrical alkane.
Count the carbons from both coupling partners and consider all pairings.
Do not confuse magnesium insertion with sodium coupling merely because both
start from an organic halide.
Some halogen compounds are studied for their properties and environmental
history as well as their reactions.
Chloroform has been used as a solvent and historically as an anaesthetic.
It has significant toxicity and can oxidize in air and light to phosgene.
Iodoform is associated with an older antiseptic use and with the yellow
product
formed in the iodoform test for suitable precursors.
Many chlorofluorocarbons persist long enough to reach the stratosphere, where
chlorine radicals can catalyse ozone destruction.
D D T has a history of insecticidal use and concerns involving persistence
and bioaccumulation.
These chemical facts should be connected with molecular stability and reaction
pathways rather than reduced to a list of names.
For a product question, record four things: substrate, reagent, solvent and
conditions.
Decide whether substitution, elimination, proton transfer or coupling is
plausible.
Check the carbon skeleton, charges and the presence of beta hydrogen where
required.
Apply a rate law only to the stated mechanism.
The practice questions review those choices; fuller stereochemical drawings
and
additional preparation routes remain for further lessons.
